guides.title: What to do when
guides.html:
Dated Thursday 19 November 2026, for your Summer 2027 applications, the summer before your senior year. Every deadline here was read off the program's own page. A program that has not posted its 2027 date is listed as not posted, never as a guess.

What changed since October. The first deadline is 4 January, not February. A run of deadlines lands between 4 and 26 January, over winter break and into the first weeks of the spring semester, and the big 1 February cluster sits right behind it. So the order of work is now:

  1. Letters, transcripts and NIH lab emails this week. All three run on somebody else's calendar.
  2. The early-January applications before you leave State College in December, while your recommenders are still easy to reach.
  3. The rest of January and the February cluster over winter break.

NIH SIP closes 26 January at noon Eastern, three weeks earlier than this site used to say. Bethesda is a commute from home, so its lack of housing costs you nothing, and NIH investigators choose their own interns, so emailing them is part of applying, not an extra.

This week: by Sunday 22 November

Open now, and close to what you want to study: NIH SIP, Seattle Children's, Penn's Undergraduate Clinical Scholars Program, Rochester's pediatric Summer Training Program, Johns Hopkins Pathway, both Indiana neuroscience programs and St. Jude, among others.

  • Finish the research version of your resume first. It goes out with every letter request and lab email. Lead your experience with the Depression and Anxiety Lab and what you do there: participant sessions, data coding, technology-based emotion tracking, protocol troubleshooting. List your three CITI certificates near the top, since most undergraduates have none. Two hours. Skeleton.
  • Ask for your letters, in this order. The PI of your Depression and Anxiety Lab first: nothing persuades like a research mentor. Then the professor whose 300-student intro psychology course you TA, who knows you as the TA who started review sessions on your own. Then the instructor of the Biology course you are a Learning Assistant for, as your backup. The pediatrician you have shadowed writes only for clinically oriented programs, as an extra letter. The first letters are due 11 January, and December is when every pre-med in the country asks. Attach the research resume and let the rest of the packet follow. How to ask.
  • Order your official transcript. Most programs take an unofficial copy, so download that PDF as well, but some insist on an official one, MSK among them. Registrar offices slow down in December and close for part of winter break, so order now. Rochester's pediatric program wants one that shows your fall 2026 grades, so order a second once those post.
  • Start NIH SIP. It is open now and closes 26 January at noon Eastern, with letters due 2 February at noon Eastern. It is one application that investigators all over NIH can read, and they start choosing their own interns in early January. Make the account and draft the cover letter this month.
  • Email three to five NIH labs, the first this week and the rest before Thanksgiving. Search NIMH (mood and anxiety), NICHD (child health) and NINDS (neurology) for labs whose recent papers you actually like, starting with any that study mood or anxiety in children. Say that you are applying through the Summer Internship Program, that you can commute from home, and when you are free, then name the same PIs in your cover letter. Template.
  • Start Seattle Children's Summer Scholars. It opened 16 November and has the earliest deadline in the cycle: 4 January at 5 p.m. Pacific, which is 8 p.m. Eastern. It needs one letter, your PI's, by 19 January. It prioritizes applicants looking for their first formal research internship, which is you, so say so.
  • Pick your list. Twelve to twenty programs is a realistic target. Sort All Programs by fit for you and read each program's For you note before you add it. Set each one to Drafting, and it moves onto My Applications, where the site tracks it for you.

Before Thanksgiving: by Wednesday 25 November

  • Give each recommender one list: every program, the date its letter is due, and how the letter gets there. The letters guide has a table to copy. Tell them how many requests to expect. Amgen alone sends a separate one for every host you choose.
  • Email the places you could commute to. Children's National, Georgetown, George Washington and Inova have not posted a 2027 summer application with a deadline, so a short email to the research training or education office is the way in, and nobody else is asking yet. Start with Children's National, the children's hospital. Its Emergency Department Clinical Research Internship runs fall to spring, but with your EMT work it is worth asking whether a summer session runs. Janelia, in Ashburn, takes summer undergraduates through HHMI's Cech Fellows Program, which recruits from partner schools: check whether Penn State is one first. Why these are worth the effort is the living-at-home rule.
  • Decide whether the MD-PhD is a real possibility. It decides which programs are worth the hours. Amgen and the Broad ask for an interest in a PhD or MD-PhD, Penn SUIP and the Leadership Alliance are built for students heading to a PhD, and Mount Sinai's SURP4US takes only future PhD and MD-PhD applicants. If the MD-PhD is real, undecided is an honest place to apply from. If not, spend those hours on the hospital programs. Penn State SURIP is out either way: it says it is not meant for students who plan to apply to medical school.

Before winter break: get the early-January applications done

The first deadlines fall while you are at home in Loudoun County and your professors are away. So the plan for December is to finish everything due by mid-January before you leave State College, or at the very least to have every letter for it requested.

  • Over Thanksgiving break, write the master personal statement. Four to six hours across a few sittings. Every application after this reuses it. The template already has your spine, how mood and anxiety show up in children, so the hours go into the part only you can write: [THE VISIT, CALL OR LAB SESSION THAT RAISED YOUR QUESTION]. Template.
  • Add the biomedical CITI course. Your human subjects and Good Clinical Practice certificates are the social and behavioral versions, and hospital studies mostly run under the biomedical track. The Biomedical Human Subjects Research course is a few hours online, usually free through your university, and it is what a children's hospital will typically ask for before you work with patient data.
  • 1 December: Yale Child Study and UMass Chan open. Yale's is child health research run with the Department of Pediatrics, squarely your area. It closes 14 January and wants two academic letters (your PI and your psychology professor) and a one-page letter of interest. It gives no housing and pays up to $4,000, only if Penn State cannot fund you first. UMass Chan closes 1 March.
  • CHOP CRISSP opens in December. No deadline is posted yet. It has a behavioral track, where your human subjects work fits, and clinical shadowing for everyone. It runs 7 June to 13 August and pays $5,000 plus free housing. Information sessions are on Tuesday 8 December, 11 a.m., and Tuesday 12 January, 3 p.m. The weekly check cannot read CHOP's page, so open it yourself every week in December.
  • Submit Seattle Children's and St. Jude POE before you leave. Most portals only email your recommenders once you submit your part, and Seattle's letter is due 19 January. St. Jude closes 1 February, but submitting in December keeps its letters clear of the January rush. It requires research experience outside the classroom, which your lab work is, and a start on 10, 17 or 24 May or 1 June.
  • Finish the 8 to 14 January applications on your list: Fred Hutch, Penn's Undergraduate Clinical Scholars Program, the Broad, UPMC Children's Pittsburgh, MD Anderson and Yale Child Study. Their dates are in the next two sections.
  • Remind your recommenders before break, with the list again and the January dates at the top. Professors are hard to reach between mid-December and the new year.

Over winter break: the first deadlines

Check your email every day. Portals send confirmations, recommenders reply, and NIH investigators start getting in touch in early January.

  • 4 January, 5 p.m. Pacific (8 p.m. Eastern): Seattle Children's. The earliest deadline in the cycle.
  • 8 January, midnight Pacific (3 a.m. Eastern on 9 January): Fred Hutch SURP. Only for students entering the summer before their final year, which is you.
  • 8 January, 5 p.m. Eastern: Penn's Undergraduate Clinical Scholars Program. Clinical research, which is rare on this list. It wants a letter from a professor and one from your research mentor: your psychology professor and your PI.
  • 10 January, 11:59 p.m. Eastern: Broad Institute BSRP. Letters by 11 January. It is for students aiming at a PhD or MD-PhD.
  • 11 January, 11:59 p.m.: UPMC Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh SRIP. The statement of purpose is all it asks for, so no letters.
  • Once your fall grades post: Rochester's pediatric Summer Training Program. It reads applications as they arrive, but it wants an official transcript with your fall 2026 grades, so have the rest ready before break. You pick the pediatric specialty and work with a mentor in it.
  • Answer NIH within a day. Investigators start choosing interns in early January, and a quick reply is part of the impression you make.
  • Draft the February applications now, because January is full of its own deadlines. With the personal statement done, each one is mostly the why-this-program paragraph, twenty to thirty minutes apiece.
  • Check the NSF REU portal. Each REU site sets its own deadline, anywhere from December to March, so look once a month. Housing and travel are usually covered.

In January: the burst

  • 13 January: MD Anderson CATALYST. $7,200 for the summer. CATALYST is an umbrella over many tracks, so read its programs page and pick yours first.
  • 14 January, 5 p.m. Eastern: Yale Child Study Center. No late applications and no extensions. The internship runs 7 June to 30 July.
  • 15 January: Mount Sinai SURP4US, Cold Spring Harbor URP (11:59 p.m. Pacific, $7,000), and both Indiana programs, INSPIRE and the Medical Neuroscience SURP. Letters for Fred Hutch, and letters and transcripts for Penn's Clinical Scholars Program, are due the same day.
  • 16 January: the earliest Vanderbilt VSSA track. Tracks close between 16 January and 15 February, most of them on 1 February, so check the date for yours.
  • 19 January: MIT MSRP. Your Seattle Children's letter is due the same day.
  • 22 January: Baylor and Texas Children's SMART. $5,400 for nine weeks.
  • 25 January, 5 p.m. Eastern: Jackson Laboratory SSP.
  • 26 January, noon Eastern: NIH SIP. The letters close a week later, on 2 February at noon.
  • 31 January: Penn State PROMISE (Hershey), with optional clinical shadowing.

Do not leave 1 February to the last week. More of this list closes that day than on any other, and it lands straight after the January burst. Have every 1 February application drafted by 20 January.

1 February to 1 March: the second wave

  • 1 February: the big cluster. Amgen Scholars (every host is its own application, and Howard, an hour from home, is one), St. Jude POE, Johns Hopkins Pathway SIP (11:59 p.m. Eastern, free housing, and a NeuroSIP division), Penn SUIP (11:59 p.m. Eastern, and your letters must arrive by the same deadline), Michigan SROP (11:59 p.m. Eastern), Stanford SSRP (11:59 p.m. Pacific), UCSF SRTP, Rockefeller SURF, Penn State SURIP, and MSK MBSP at 8 a.m., not end of day.
  • 2 February, noon Eastern: your NIH SIP letters. NYU Langone SURP closes the same day, but it requires a full semester of bench research, and yours has been with people, not at a bench, so leave it off.
  • 3 February: Leadership Alliance and Mayo Clinic SURF. The Leadership Alliance ranks three of its 20 sites on one application, and Howard is the only one you could commute to. At Mayo you pick a research area, and neuroscience is one.
  • 12 February: ECU Brody SBRP.
  • 15 February, noon Eastern: Penn State AHA-USF (Hershey, $6,000, housing at your own cost), with your letter and transcript in by the same noon. The last Vanderbilt tracks close that day too.
  • 1 March: UMass Chan SURP. $6,000 plus travel and housing.

Not posted yet: check these by hand

These have no 2027 deadline on their page yet. If the site shows a date for one, it is an estimate, marked est.

  • CHOP CRISSP, opening in December (above).
  • Children's National, about an hour from home, and Kennedy Krieger and Johns Hopkins JHIBS in Baltimore, a long commute at about 70 minutes each way. Kennedy Krieger studies developmental disabilities and neurodevelopment, the research side of developmental and behavioral pediatrics.
  • Cincinnati Children's SURF, from your original list.
  • Caltech SURF. The application is a research proposal written with a prospective mentor, so that contact has to happen weeks before the deadline.
  • The rest are on the Timeline page. The weekly check flags a page when it changes, which is usually a program posting its dates. A few sites block the check, CHOP among them, and The Plan lists those for you to open by hand.

Off the list

  • SHPEP has ended. Its funder closed it, and the last cohort ran in summer 2026.
  • NYSCF requires New York City residency, so it is not open to you.
  • The Allen Institute now lists only ASPIRE, a year-long postbaccalaureate role, not a summer internship.
  • Columbia's Zuckerman Institute runs its summer programs only for Columbia and Barnard students.
  • CHLA's summer student program page is gone. The only undergraduate route there now is NIDDK's national STEP-UP program.

March to April: decisions

Decisions arrive from early March to mid-April. The Broad and Fred Hutch decide by mid-March, and Michigan by 5 April. MD Anderson wants an answer to its offers by 4 March, before many programs have decided, so know your order of preference before then.

If nothing lands: direct emails to PIs and Penn State's own summer research funding are both still live in April. A summer with a real project, in your own lab or one near home, is worth more than a prestigious program you did not get.

The honest summary

Four things decide this cycle, in order:

  1. Letters asked for this week, your PI first, with the research resume attached. The only item gated on someone else.
  2. The early-January applications finished before winter break. Seattle Children's closes 4 January, while you are at home.
  3. Emails to PIs, NIH first, starting this week. NIH investigators choose their own interns, and NIH is a commute from home.
  4. Not cramming 1 February. Draft that cluster over winter break.

Everything else is execution.

guides.title: How to get picked
guides.html:
Useful context for where to spend your effort. None of this is a secret. It is just not written down anywhere an applicant naturally looks. Your own strengths and gaps come near the end.

Who reads the application

For a program with its own selection committee (CHOP, St. Jude), it is usually two stages:

  1. A screen against hard criteria: eligibility rules such as citizenship and class year, and completeness. This stage is mechanical. Most rejections happen here and have nothing to do with how good the applicant is.
  2. Faculty review. Files get routed to labs by research area. A PI scans for: does this person want to do what we do, and can they be useful for ten weeks?

The second stage is the one worth optimizing for, and it hinges on specificity. Your record already answers the second question better than most. The work goes into the first, answered separately for each lab.

NIH SIP works differently. There is no central committee: individual NIH investigators read the applicant pool and choose their own interns, starting in early January. Your cover letter and your emails to PIs do most of the work there, which is why the cold email matters most at NIH. NIH is also a commute from home, and NICHD (child health), NIMH (mood and anxiety) and NINDS (neurology) between them cover what you want to study.

What the screen is checking

Failing any of these wastes the whole application:

  • What you plan to do next. Amgen and the Broad ask for an interest in a PhD or MD-PhD, Penn SUIP and the Leadership Alliance are built for students heading to a PhD, and Penn State SURIP says it is not meant for students who plan to apply to medical school. You are premed and still deciding between an MD and an MD-PhD, so this is the screen to think hardest about. What to do about it is under your gaps, below.
  • Research experience already done. St. Jude POE requires research experience outside the classroom when you apply, and your lab work is exactly that. NYU Langone SURP wants at least one full semester of bench lab research. Yours is with people, not at a bench, so that one is out this cycle.
  • Class year. Never a problem for you. Every program on the site takes juniors, and Fred Hutch takes only students entering the summer before their final year, which is you.
  • Availability for the full term. St. Jude requires one of four start dates (10, 17 or 24 May, or 1 June) and eleven weeks from undergraduates. The Broad requires all nine weeks, with no other courses or job. If anything else claims part of your summer, such as an MCAT date, raise it before applying, not after.
  • Completeness. Letters that arrive after the deadline sink otherwise strong applications. Penn SUIP's letters, for one, must arrive by the application deadline itself.
  • Citizenship and residency. As a US citizen you clear every citizenship rule on this list. Residency is the exception: NYSCF takes only New York City residents, which is why it is off your list.

The site's filters exist mostly to stop you spending four hours on a program you are not eligible for. Fill in My eligibility and the site flags every program that conflicts, with the reason.

What the faculty review is weighing

Roughly in order:

  1. Fit with a specific lab. The single biggest factor, and the one most within your control. An application that names a PI, references their work, and says why, lands in a different pile. If you have emailed that PI and they said yes, it is a different pile again.
  2. Evidence of follow-through. Ten weeks is short. They are looking for signs someone will not need babysitting: a project you ran, a protocol you handled, a semester of consistent lab hours, a job that required showing up. This is your strongest ground (see what you bring, below).
  3. A real reason for the area. Not passion, a question, specific enough to tell a reader where to route the file. One could grow straight out of your lab: how mood and anxiety disorders show up in children, and whether emotion tracking like your lab's could pick them up. Write yours in one sentence: [your question].
  4. Letters. Mostly used as corroboration. A detailed letter from someone who supervised you beats a glowing one from someone who taught you in a lecture. For you, that is whoever supervises your lab work, then a professor who has watched you up close, such as the one whose course you TA.
  5. Coursework. It matters less here than at the screen, as long as the relevant courses are there, and yours are: general and organic chemistry, biochemistry, physics, calculus and psychology.

What does not move the needle

  • Enthusiasm as such. Everyone is enthusiastic.
  • Volume of extracurriculars unrelated to research or clinical work.
  • Prestige-signaling about the program in the essay. They know it is good.
  • A longer personal statement. Over-length is a mild negative.
  • A long case for why you want to be a doctor. Here your clinical work is evidence that you are reliable, not the subject: a research program is choosing a researcher.

The four asymmetries worth exploiting

One application, many labs. NIH SIP and Vanderbilt's VSSA each put a single application in front of many labs. Investigators all over NIH can read your SIP application, and VSSA runs many tracks through one portal. The marginal cost of the second, third and fifth lab is small, so do these first and do them well. The Leadership Alliance works the same way, ranking three of its 20 sites from one application, but it says it is not designed for clinical medicine careers, so it belongs on your list only if an MD-PhD becomes a firm plan.

Amgen Scholars is the near miss. There is no single Amgen application: each of the 14 US hosts runs its own, with its own portal and its own letter request to your recommenders. The essays are reusable and the paperwork is not, so count each extra host as half an application rather than a free one, and tell your recommenders how many there will be.

Cold emails. Fifteen minutes, and the only thing that converts an anonymous file into a named candidate. Most applicants never send one. At NIH they are part of the application, and near home they are often the only way in: Inova and Georgetown post pages about research and training, not summer applications with deadlines. Template.

Less-famous places with real research. Arkansas Children's, Stowers, Van Andel, UAB, Einstein, Nemours and Benaroya do genuine work and receive a fraction of the applications that CHOP and St. Jude get. A summer with a real project and a mentor who had time beats a rejection from a famous program. Build the list with a few of these in it deliberately. Arkansas Children's and Nemours are pediatric. The rest lean toward basic science, so read the For you note on each before you commit the hours.

Living at home. A program you can commute to is worth more than its stipend says, because none of it goes on rent. From home you can reach NIH in Bethesda, Janelia in Ashburn, Inova in Fairfax, and Children's National, Georgetown, George Washington and Howard in Washington. Baltimore, for Johns Hopkins, Kennedy Krieger and the University of Maryland, is about 70 minutes each way: possible, but a long commute. The Can live at home filter in All Programs lists them all. See the living-at-home rule.

Your strengths and your gaps

What you bring

  • More than a year of human-subjects research. Since August 2025 you have run participant sessions, coded data, worked on technology-based emotion tracking and troubleshot study protocols. Describe it in verbs, and add the one problem you solved: [a protocol problem, and what you changed].
  • Three CITI certificates. Most undergraduates have none. Put them near the top of your CV, where a human-subjects lab will see them first.
  • Far more patient contact than most applicants. More than 100 emergency calls as a volunteer EMT, about 12 hours a week on top of classes, and a summer as a medical assistant seeing up to 26 patients a day. In clinical research that transfers directly, and anywhere else it is evidence that you show up. Give the numbers every time.
  • Two teaching roles. Biology Learning Assistant for 80 students, and Psychology TA for a 300-student course where you started review sessions yourself. That is the initiative a PI hopes for in a summer student.
  • More than five years of shadowing a pediatrician. This is what makes your interest in children believable. Use it to open a question rather than to prove commitment: [a moment from shadowing that left you with a question].

The gaps, and what to do about each

  • No bench experience. It rules out NYU Langone, and Harvard SHURP asks for a semester of college-level lab research, so ask whether a psychology lab counts before you spend the hours. Elsewhere the bench is something you would learn, not a screen. St. Jude, for one, places undergraduates only in laboratory or computational work. Say plainly that it would be new, and what carries over: following protocols exactly, coding data carefully, fixing a procedure when it breaks. Then aim a good share of your list at research with people, where your experience is the job itself, such as CHOP's clinical and behavioral tracks. The fit rating on each program weighs exactly this.
  • No poster yet. Normal before a first summer program, and several of these programs end with one: Rochester's Strong Children's Research Center program and Einstein both close with a poster session. Meanwhile, ask your PI whether any of the lab's work could become a poster this spring with you on it. If an abstract is accepted, it goes on your CV that day.
  • Premed, where some programs want future PhDs. Penn State SURIP is out either way, since an MD-PhD is still medical school. For Amgen, the Broad and Penn SUIP, decide where an MD-PhD really stands. If it is a real possibility, they are a fair test of it, and you can say exactly that: you are deciding, and want the summer to help. If you lean toward an MD alone, spend those hours on programs open to future physicians, such as Penn's Undergraduate Clinical Scholars Program, which says it is built for students aiming at an MD, PhD or MD-PhD. Never claim a PhD plan you do not have: an interview will find it out.

What does not help, with any of the three: apologizing in your personal statement.

A realistic expectation

These programs run acceptance rates in the low single digits to low teens. Strong applicants get rejected from most places they apply. The right response is volume on the reusable applications plus a handful of genuinely attainable targets, not six perfect applications to six famous programs.

Twelve to twenty applications is a reasonable target for this cycle, and this site is built to make that a realistic amount of work rather than an impossible one.

guides.title: Reading a program page
guides.html:
Program pages bury the things that decide whether an application is worth starting. This is the order to look for them.

The five disqualifiers. Check these first

Before reading a single word about the research, find:

  1. Citizenship requirement. "US citizen or permanent resident" appears on most federally funded programs. As a US citizen you clear this one, so look for residency rules instead: NYSCF takes only New York City residents, which is why it is no longer on the site.
  2. Class year. Look for "rising senior", "must have completed sophomore year", "may not graduate before/during the program". In summer 2027 you are a rising senior who graduates in May 2028. Every program on the site takes that year, and Fred Hutch takes no other, so this check is for programs you find elsewhere.
  3. Degree goal. Some programs exist to send students on to a PhD or an MD-PhD. The Broad asks that you be aiming at one, and Penn SUIP and Amgen are built for students who are. You have not decided between an MD and an MD-PhD. As long as the MD-PhD is a real possibility, undecided is an honest place to apply from, so say so plainly. If you settle on the MD alone, the Broad is out and the PhD-track programs drop down your list. Penn State SURIP is out either way: it says it is not meant for students headed to medical school, and an MD-PhD is still medical school.
  4. Dates. Fixed start dates (St. Jude has four and only four), and whether the full term is mandatory. Some programs also rule out any other job or class: the Broad and the University of Maryland's Schnaper program (NSIP) both do, so a summer at either means no EMT or medical assistant job on the side, and no summer course.
  5. Deadline, and what it covers. Specifically: are letters due on the same date, or later? Penn SUIP and the Schnaper program both want letters in by the application deadline itself. The Broad gives letters one extra day, and Seattle Children's gives them fifteen. Read the hour too: NIH SIP closes at noon Eastern on January 26, not at midnight.

If any of these rule you out, stop. That is a win, four hours saved.

Then find the mentor list

The most valuable page on any program site, and often two clicks deep: "Faculty", "Mentors", "Research areas", "Labs", or a PDF of last year's projects.

Every program on this site carries a fit rating, and its For you note says how the program lines up with what you have done and want to study. The mentor list is where you check that. Search it for your own words: child, adolescent, development, behavior, anxiety, depression, mood, emotion, neurology. A lab that studies how mood and anxiety show up in children, or that runs studies with people, is one where you are useful from the first week. You already run participant sessions and code data, and you hold three CITI certificates where most undergraduates have none.

Check, too, what undergraduates actually do there. St. Jude places undergraduates in laboratory or computational projects and keeps clinical research for medical students. All of your research so far has been with people, not at a bench, so at a program like that the bench would be new. Say so, and point to what carries over: following a protocol exactly, coding data carefully and troubleshooting a procedure when it fails.

This is where the why-this-program paragraph and the cold emails come from. A program with no published mentor list is one where naming a mentor matters less, and a program with a long list is one where naming a mentor matters a great deal.

Then the practicalities

  • Stipend, and whether housing is separate. The two numbers only mean something together. Jackson Lab at Bar Harbor pays $7,500 with room, board and travel included. Fred Hutch pays $7,304 and leaves housing to you, about $3,400 at UW. The stipends are nearly the same, but after rent the Fred Hutch one is worth about half as much.
  • Housing: provided, subsidized, or your problem. "Not provided" is only bad news if you have to pay rent, which is what the living-at-home rule below is about.
  • Travel: Jackson Lab and some others cover it; most do not.
  • Length: usually ten weeks, sometimes eight or nine (St. Jude wants eleven from undergraduates), and whether it collides with the end of your spring semester at Penn State.

The dataset already has all of this, but verify it on the page before applying. The stipend figures in particular are the fields most likely to be stale.

The living-at-home rule

A program you can commute to from home is worth a smaller stipend, because housing is free at home. With no rent to pay, a stipend with no housing is the whole stipend. The same offer in Seattle, Boston or New York can lose close to half of it to rent, as the Fred Hutch numbers above show.

From home in Loudoun County, without traffic:

  • Janelia in Ashburn: 10 to 20 minutes. Its summer undergraduates come through HHMI's Cech Fellows Program, which recruits from partner schools, so check whether Penn State is one before anything else.
  • Inova in Fairfax: 30 to 40 minutes. No housing, and you need none.
  • NIH in Bethesda: 40 to 50 minutes. NIH SIP provides no housing, which does not matter when you are driving in from home.
  • Children's National, Georgetown, George Washington and Howard in DC: 45 minutes to an hour. Children's National and GW give no housing, which is fine from home.
  • Johns Hopkins, Kennedy Krieger and the University of Maryland in Baltimore: 70 to 80 minutes each way. Here a program with no housing costs you something real: about two and a half hours in the car every day, or rent. Hopkins Pathway houses its interns free, the Schnaper program offers campus housing (ask what it costs), and Kennedy Krieger gives none.

Rush hour adds a lot to all of these, most of all on the drives into DC and Baltimore, so check each drive at the hour you would actually make it. The Can live at home filter on All Programs lists every program the site counts as within reach.

So when you compare offers, compare what you keep: the stipend, less rent where you would pay it, or less gas and parking where you would drive. A smaller stipend near home can beat a bigger one in a city where you pay rent.

Signs the page is from a previous cycle

Still common, because plenty of 2027 pages have not been updated yet:

  • Dates in 2025 or 2026 with no mention of 2027
  • "Applications are closed", "check back in the fall", "will open in November"
  • A deadline that has already passed

None of these mean the program is gone. They mean the new cycle is not posted. Note the date and let the weekly check catch the update. You do not have to run anything: it runs every Monday on its own, and what it found sits at the top of The Plan. A page that changes, and especially one that starts mentioning 2027, is usually a program posting its new dates.

One thing it cannot do. Some sites refuse an automated reader, so the check never sees them at all. CHOP CRISSP is one of them, and one to watch: its page says it opens in December, and it runs a behavioral track alongside the basic and clinical ones. The Plan lists every one under the note that says those sites block the weekly check. Open those pages yourself every couple of weeks, because nothing is going to tell you when they post.

When the page says almost nothing

Some real programs have one thin paragraph and an email address. That is not a bad sign. It often means placements are arranged directly rather than through a portal, which is good news for you: more than a year of running participant sessions and coding data is exactly what a short email can show.

In that case skip the application entirely and go straight to a cold email to the listed contact or to a relevant PI. UCSF pediatrics and the UC Davis MIND Institute work this way, and so do three of the places you could commute to. Georgetown, George Washington and Inova post a page about research and training rather than a summer application with a deadline. GW's pediatrics department is based at Children's National, so an email there can reach the same hospital by another route. And Inova is in Fairfax, where you worked as a medical assistant last summer: if anyone you met there knows someone at Inova, an introduction beats a cold email.

guides.title: Personal statement
guides.html:
Write this once, properly. Then every application becomes: paste the master, swap the program-specific paragraph, adjust length. That is the difference between applying to six programs and applying to twenty.

Target length: 600-800 words. Most programs ask for 500-1000, and a tight 650 reads better than a padded 950.

Write it over Thanksgiving break. Seattle Children's, your earliest deadline, closes January 4, 2027.

Your statement already has a spine. More than five years of shadowing a pediatrician and over a year in the Depression and Anxiety Lab at Penn State meet in one question: how mood and anxiety disorders show up in children. Paragraphs 1 to 3 below follow that line.

The shape

Paragraph 1, why pediatrics (100-150 words)

Not "I have always loved working with children." Your root is more than five years of shadowing a pediatrician. Do not summarize the years: pick one visit, the thing you noticed, and the question it left you with.

Weak: "Shadowing a pediatrician for more than five years has shown me how much I love caring for children."

Better: "[ONE VISIT FROM THOSE YEARS]. What stuck with me was not [the obvious part] but [the specific thing you noticed]. I wanted to know [the actual question]."

If a visit showed you how worry or low mood looks in a child, it leads straight into paragraphs 2 and 3, but use it only if it happened. A personal reason behind the pediatric interest goes here too, stated plainly, once, without reaching for drama.

Paragraph 2, what the lab has taught you (150-200 words)

Lead with the Depression and Anxiety Lab: what it is asking (how mood disorders show up in movement and affect), what you do there, and what that has taught you about doing research, not just what the project is about.

Committees read for evidence that someone can be trusted with ten weeks of a mentor's time: running something independently, handling a protocol, dealing with something that did not work. You have all three. You run participant sessions, you troubleshoot study protocols when they break, and you started review sessions for a 300-student psychology course on your own. Tell one instance properly.

"In the Depression and Anxiety Lab at Penn State, I [WHAT YOU DO, in plain verbs: run participant sessions, code data, troubleshoot the protocol]. [ONE TIME A SESSION OR THE PROTOCOL DID NOT GO AS PLANNED, AND WHAT YOU DID]. That taught me [SOMETHING REAL ABOUT RESEARCH, not a platitude]."

Then a clause or a sentence each:

  • CITI training: Students in Research, Social and Behavioral Human Subjects Research, and Good Clinical Practice. Most undergraduates have none of these, and they tell a mentor running human-subjects studies that you know the rules.
  • Clinical work, for what it shows a mentor: up to 26 patients a day as a medical assistant says you are accurate at volume, and more than 100 emergency calls as a volunteer EMT says you follow procedure under pressure. The rest stays on the CV.
  • What you do not have, said plainly: bench experience, posters, publications. Do not apologize or imply otherwise. For a bench lab, one sentence covers it: your research so far is with human subjects, you have taken organic chemistry and biochemistry, and [WHAT CARRIES OVER TO THE BENCH].

Paragraph 3, what you want to learn next (120-180 words)

The research area, and why. Be specific enough that a reader could guess which labs to route the application to. Yours is where pediatrics and developmental psychology meet: how mood and anxiety disorders show up in children. "Pediatric research" tells a reader nothing; "how anxiety shows up in children's behavior, and how early it can be seen" tells them where to send the file.

The bridge from paragraph 2 is already built. Your lab studies how mood disorders show up in movement and affect, so ask what that looks like in a child: [YOUR QUESTION, in your words]. Then say what the summer would teach you that your lab cannot: [WHAT IT WOULD ADD, such as working with children and families].

Naming a method helps: yours (participant sessions, data coding, technology-based emotion tracking), and the lab's, such as EEG or patient-registry data, once you have read its papers.

Keep mood and anxiety in children at the center and tilt it per program, toward neuroscience or pediatric neurology for a brain sciences program and toward clinical research for a clinical one. Tilting is fine; a new interest for every program is not.

Paragraph 4, why this program, specifically (100-150 words)

The one paragraph that changes every time. See the why-this-program guide. Never send an application where this paragraph could have been addressed to any other institution. The For you line on each program is a fair place to start, but the paragraph still needs a lab, a person or a paper from that program.

Paragraph 5, where this goes (80-120 words)

You are headed for medicine and have not decided between an MD and an MD-PhD. Undecided is a fine answer. What is not fine is vagueness that reads as not having thought about it, so say what the summer would help you decide.

"I plan to become a physician, and I have not yet decided whether that means an MD or an MD-PhD. This summer would tell me [WHAT YOU WANT TO FIND OUT]."

Amgen Scholars, the Broad, Penn SUIP, the Leadership Alliance, MIT MSRP and WashU's BioMedRAP are PhD-pipeline programs. The first four also count an MD-PhD, so they are open to you if that question is real; say so honestly rather than writing yourself as PhD-bound. Penn State SURIP says it is not meant for students who plan to apply to medical school, which you will do either way. If you land on MD-only, those hours belong to the hospital-based programs, and the statement should not pretend otherwise.

Three that need a different shape

Most applications take the master with paragraph 4 swapped. These do not:

  • The Broad wants five short essays, not one statement (closes January 10, 2027). Build them from your paragraphs.
  • UPMC Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh asks for nothing but a statement of purpose (closes January 11, 2027), so it carries your lab work, CITI training and clinical hours on its own.
  • Yale Child Study Center wants a one-page letter of interest (closes January 14, 2027). It is a developmental science internship, so keep paragraphs 3 and 4 nearly whole and cut the rest to a sentence or two each.

Before sending, check

  • Could another premed with shadowing hours have written this paragraph? Rewrite it.
  • Does the program name appear, spelled correctly, in paragraph 4?
  • Is there at least one specific paper, lab or faculty member named?
  • Any sentence about loving science or children? Replace it with something you saw or did.
  • Could anyone identify a patient or participant you mention? Cut the detail.
  • Does anything imply bench work, a poster or a publication? Fix it.
  • Read it aloud. Anywhere you stumble, a reader will too.
  • Within the word limit. Over-length gets cut or counted against.
  • Someone else proofread it. Not spellcheck, a person.

Three openings that work

  1. The question. Open with what you want to know about mood and anxiety in children, then how you came to care about it.
  2. The moment. One visit from your years of shadowing, and the question it raised. An EMT call or a patient from your medical assistant summer can work too, but only if it leads to your research question, not just to medicine.
  3. The problem. Something unresolved about how mood disorders show up in children, and where you want to stand in relation to it. Strongest if you have read the papers behind your lab's work; risky if you have not.

Avoid: quotations from famous scientists, dictionary definitions, "Webster's defines", and childhood-illness framing unless it is genuinely yours to tell.

guides.title: CV skeleton
guides.html:
One page, and you have more than enough to fill it: a lab, five certifications, three clinical roles, more than five years of shadowing and two teaching roles. The work is in the order and the bullets, not in finding things to say. Your letter requests and your emails to labs both attach this CV, so finish it before you send either.

A research CV is not a job resume. The resume you have now was built for clinical jobs: the lab is one line near the bottom and the CITI training is not on it at all. This version turns that around, with education first, then the lab in full, then the certificates, then the clinical work and the teaching. Leave off any objective statement, and any line that just says "Microsoft Office".

Wherever the CV below says [TAB], the part after it sits flush against the right margin. How to do that in Google Docs or Word, without spaces, is the first rule under the CV.

[FULL NAME]
[email] · [phone] · [home city, state] · [LinkedIn, optional]


EDUCATION

The Pennsylvania State University [TAB] University Park, PA
Bachelor of Science in Integrative Science, expected May 2028 [TAB] GPA: [GPA]
Minor in Psychology
Alpha Epsilon Delta, premedical honor society [TAB] [Year joined]
[Any other honors or scholarships]


RESEARCH EXPERIENCE

Research Assistant, Depression and Anxiety Lab [TAB] Aug 2025 to present
Department of Psychology, Penn State. Supervisor: [Dr. Name]
· Lab focus: how mood disorders show up in movement and affect.
· Run participant sessions [how many so far, your hours a week, and whether
  you run them alone].
· Code study data [what kind of data, and with what scheme or software].
· [Your part in the lab's technology-based emotion tracking, starting
  with a verb.]
· Troubleshoot study protocols [one problem you solved, and what changed].


CERTIFICATIONS

CITI Program: Students in Research [TAB] [Month Year]
CITI Program: Social and Behavioral Human Subjects Research [TAB] [Month Year]
CITI Program: Good Clinical Practice (Social and Behavioral) [TAB] [Month Year]
EMT-Basic, National Registry (NREMT), licensed in Virginia [TAB] [Month Year]
Basic Life Support (BLS), [issuer] [TAB] [Month Year]


CLINICAL EXPERIENCE AND SHADOWING

Volunteer EMT, Centre LifeLink EMS, State College, PA [TAB] Aug 2025 to present
· Respond to emergency calls, more than 100 so far, about 12 hours a week.
· [What you do on a call, starting with a verb.]

Medical Assistant, [family medicine practice], Fairfax, VA [TAB] Summer 2026
· Took vital signs, drew blood, gave vaccines and charted for up to 26
  patients a day.

Sports Medicine EMT, [facility name], Springfield, VA [TAB] May 2025 to Feb 2026
· [What you handled, with a number if you have one.]

Lifeguard, [employer], [City, State] [TAB] [Month Year] to [Month Year]

Pediatric Shadowing, [Dr. Name, practice] [TAB] [Year] to [Year, or present]
· [Total hours, roughly] over more than five years.


TEACHING EXPERIENCE

Psychology Teaching Assistant, Penn State [TAB] [Month Year] to present
· Started review sessions for a 300-student introductory course on own
  initiative [how often they run, and how many students come].
· [What else the role covers, starting with a verb.]

Biology Learning Assistant, Penn State [TAB] [Month Year] to present
· [What you do in the role, starting with a verb], for 80 students.


SKILLS

Research: participant sessions, data coding, technology-based emotion
tracking, protocol troubleshooting
Clinical: vital signs, blood draws, vaccine administration, charting, BLS
Software: [only what you have used yourself, such as Excel, SPSS, R or REDCap]
Languages: [any besides English, with your level, or delete this line]


RELEVANT COURSEWORK

Biochemistry, Organic Chemistry, [your psychology courses, by name],
[statistics or research methods, if taken], General Chemistry, Physics, Calculus

Everything outside the square brackets comes from what you have already done. The brackets are the parts only you can fill in: names, dates, counts, and what you do in the lab day to day, which matters most.

Rules that matter

  • Do not fake the right-hand column with spaces. The CV marks it with [TAB] because spaces do not survive the trip into a word processor: in Google Docs or Word every run of spaces lands somewhere different and the right edge comes out ragged. Use a right-aligned tab stop. In Google Docs, click the ruler at the right margin and add a right tab stop there. In Word, open the Paragraph settings, choose Tabs, and set a right-aligned tab at the right margin. Then press Tab once wherever the CV says [TAB]. A two-column table with the borders turned off works too. Both survive editing and the PDF export.
  • Use the bullet button for the · lines instead of typing the dots, so a bullet that wraps onto a second line stays indented.
  • Reverse chronological within every section, with the roles you still hold first.
  • Present tense for what you still do, past tense for what you have finished. "Run participant sessions" for the lab, "Took vital signs" for the summer job.
  • No pronouns. "Code study data," not "I code study data."
  • Verbs first. Not "Responsible for troubleshooting study protocols" but "Troubleshoot study protocols."
  • Be specific about skills. "Experience with research participants" says little. "Participant sessions, data coding, protocol troubleshooting" says more, and the name of the software or coding scheme says more still. List only what you could do unsupervised tomorrow.
  • Quantify where it is honest. You already have numbers most applicants do not: more than 100 emergency calls, up to 26 patients a day, 80 students as a Learning Assistant and a 300-student course as a TA. The lab entry needs its own, such as sessions run and hours a week.
  • Certifications near the top. Most undergraduate applicants have no CITI training, and you have three certificates, Good Clinical Practice among them. Here they sit right under your research, where a human-subjects lab sees them first. Copy each course title exactly as it reads on the certificate. If you add the biomedical CITI course this winter, it goes with them.
  • Coursework: the four to six courses that matter most. Biochemistry and organic chemistry lead, then your psychology courses by name and any statistics or research methods. General chemistry, physics and calculus are on every premed transcript, so they go last, and they come off first if the list runs past two lines.
  • One page, 10-11pt, generous margins. A cramped two-pager reads worse than a clean one-pager. If yours runs over, cut the lifeguard line first, then shorten the clinical bullets, and leave the lab alone. Yale Child Study Center asks for a two-page resume, so for that one application you can put the cut detail back.
  • Home on the contact line. For the city, use home in Loudoun County rather than State College. For a program or lab near home, that tells the reader you would commute and need no housing: the living-at-home rule at work.
  • Export to PDF, named Lastname-Firstname-CV.pdf. Never send a .docx.

One lab, no bench work, no posters yet

That is a normal research section for the summer before senior year, and plenty of programs on the site take students with no bench experience at all. Seattle Children's says prior research experience is not required and prioritizes first-time research interns. For developmental and clinical research, where your interests point, participant sessions and CITI training are the right experience, not a stand-in for bench work.

  • Write the lab entry in full. It is the entry a research program reads most closely, so give it every bullet it can honestly carry. More than a year in one lab is the follow-through a reviewer looks for.
  • A real course project counts too. If a course had you ask a question and collect or analyze data to answer it, give it its own entry under the lab: the question, and what you did. A lab course that followed set procedures is coursework, not research.
  • Leave bench techniques off. You have not done bench work, and anything on the page is fair game in an interview. Do not dress the human-subjects work up in bench language either. For a bench program, let the coursework line speak instead: organic chemistry and biochemistry show you have the background. If a program wants bench experience, read its fit rating and the For you note on the site before you spend the hours.
  • No presentations or publications section yet. Add one the day a poster or abstract is accepted, and not before: an empty or padded section reads worse than none. A poster at a campus symposium counts. List the authors in the order on the abstract, then the title, where and when it was presented, and whether it was a poster or a talk.
  • Leave high-school material off. The shadowing is the exception: more than five years with one pediatrician earns its line.

guides.title: Asking for letters
guides.html:
Most programs that ask for letters want two, and some want one. Your two are your PI and the professor of the psychology course you TA. The same two letters go everywhere, so this is a one-time cost, but only if you ask early and make it easy.

Ask as soon as you read this. The first letters are due in mid-January. Yale Child Study Center's application, which needs two academic letters, closes 14 January at 5 p.m. Eastern. Penn's Undergraduate Clinical Scholars Program wants its letters sent by 15 January at 5 p.m. Eastern, and Seattle Children's by 19 January. Faculty write letters in batches, and December is when every premed in the country is asking. A request in November gives them weeks. One sent in January does not.

Who to ask

In order of usefulness:

  1. Your PI in the Depression and Anxiety Lab. Nothing else is as persuasive, and you have been running participant sessions, coding data and troubleshooting protocols in that lab since August 2025. Where a program takes one letter, as Seattle Children's does, this is the one. If a graduate student or postdoc supervises you day to day, ask whether they can write it with your PI, since the detail comes from whoever watched you work.
  2. The professor of the intro psychology course you TA. A 300-student lecture is usually a poor source of letters, but you are not one of the 300. You work for this professor, who watched you start the review sessions on your own.
  3. The instructor of the Biology course you are a Learning Assistant for. They have watched you show up for 80 students and follow through, which is most of what a letter is for. They are also your backup: if either of the first two says no, or has not answered in a week, ask straight away.
  4. For clinically oriented programs only: the pediatrician you have shadowed for more than five years, or an EMS supervisor at Centre LifeLink. The pediatrician can vouch for more than five years of interest in pediatrics, a supervisor for your own work on more than 100 emergency calls. Use one as a second or extra letter, never in place of your PI's, and only where the program does not ask for academic or faculty letters.

Your first two fit the programs that say who should write: Yale Child Study Center wants two academic letters, Rochester's Strong Children's Research Center two faculty letters, and Penn's Clinical Scholars Program one from a professor and one from your research mentor.

Avoid a famous professor who cannot pick you out of a crowd. You have three people who can. If you ever need a fourth, choose a professor from a small, hard course where you spoke up, not a big lecture you sat in.

The email

Ask in person where you can, then send this the same day. This version is for your PI.

Subject: Letter of recommendation request, summer 2027 research programs (first letter due [EARLIEST LETTER DATE])

Dear Dr. [LAST NAME],

I am applying to summer 2027 research programs, mostly in pediatric, developmental and clinical research, and I am hoping you would be willing to write me a letter of recommendation.

I have been a research assistant in your lab since August 2025. I run participant sessions, code data, work on the technology-based emotion tracking and troubleshoot study protocols. [ONE THING YOU NOW HANDLE ON YOUR OWN, AND SINCE WHEN.]

I am applying to about [NUMBER] programs. The first letter is due [EARLIEST LETTER DATE] and the last on [LATEST LETTER DATE]. Most programs collect letters through an online form that emails you a link once I submit my part, so you would get one email per program. I have attached the list, with each date and how each letter is submitted, and I will send a reminder before every deadline so you do not have to track any of it.

I have also attached my CV, my draft personal statement, and a short note on the parts of my work you may not have seen.

Would you be willing? If you do not feel you could write a strong letter, I would completely understand. I would rather know now.

Thank you for considering it.

[YOUR NAME]

Fill both dates from your own list. If the Broad is on it, the first letter is due 11 January.

The paragraph asking whether they could write a strong letter matters. It gives a lukewarm writer a graceful exit, which is far better than a tepid letter you never see.

For the others, change the greeting to the title each one goes by, and swap the paragraph about the lab for theirs:

The psychology professor: I have been a teaching assistant for your [COURSE NUMBER] since [TERM], and I started its review sessions myself. [WHEN THEY RUN AND ROUGHLY HOW MANY OF THE 300 STUDENTS COME.]

The Biology instructor: I have been a Learning Assistant for your [COURSE NUMBER] since [TERM], working with its 80 students. [ONE THING THEY HAVE SEEN YOU DO IN THAT ROLE.]

The pediatrician: I have shadowed you since [YEAR]. [ONE THING YOU LEARNED WHILE SHADOWING, WITH NOTHING THAT COULD IDENTIFY A PATIENT.]

An EMS supervisor: I have volunteered with Centre LifeLink since August 2025 and answered more than 100 emergency calls. [ONE CALL OR SHIFT THEY SAW YOU HANDLE, WITH NOTHING THAT COULD IDENTIFY A PATIENT.]

A clinical writer is writing for one or two programs, not all of them, so replace the paragraph about how many programs with their names and dates.

If your personal statement is not drafted yet, send the request anyway with the CV and say the statement will follow within two weeks. Waiting for a perfect packet costs more than it gains.

The one list to send each recommender

One page, one row per program, in date order. It is the most useful thing you can give a recommender, because it turns twenty separate emails into one plan. Copy this table and fill in your own programs. The date comes from the program's page on the site, and how the letter is submitted comes from the program's own page. Where a page gives no separate date for letters, use the application deadline.

ProgramLetter dueHow the letter is submitted
Yale Child Study Center internship14 January, 5 p.m. Eastern (the application deadline)[a link the portal emails them, an upload, or an email address]
Penn Undergraduate Clinical Scholars Program15 January, 5 p.m. Eastern, sent or postmarked[how]
Seattle Children's Summer Scholars19 January, [time and time zone][how]
NIH Summer Internship Program2 February, noon Eastern[how]
[Program][Date, time and time zone][how]

The filled rows are real dates. Keep the ones you are applying to and add the rest, but only programs you mean to finish: every row is another form for a writer. If you are not sure a program is worth a row, its fit rating and the For you line on its page are a quick check.

Three things make the list work:

  • Put the time and time zone on every date. NIH's letters close at noon Eastern on 2 February, and a professor who reads "2 February" will assume the end of the day.
  • Give each Amgen host its own row. Each host runs its own application, so five hosts means five requests.
  • Flag the ones where letters are due with the application, so they get done first. Penn SUIP and the University of Maryland's Schnaper program both want everything, letters included, by 1 February.

The packet to attach

Everything that makes writing easier makes the letter better:

  1. CV: the research version, with the lab first and your three CITI certificates on it. The CV guide has yours laid out. Most undergraduates have no CITI training, and a writer who sees yours can say so.
  2. Personal statement: the draft is fine. It tells them the story to corroborate.
  3. Their rows of the one list, not the whole spreadsheet from the site. Your PI's has every program. The psychology professor's leaves out the programs that take one letter, since that letter is your PI's. A clinical writer's has only the programs it is for.
  4. What they have not seen. Each writer knows one part of what you do. Your PI may not know about your 100-plus calls with Centre LifeLink, the summer as a medical assistant seeing up to 26 patients a day, or the years of shadowing, and your instructors may not know about the lab. One short paragraph with those numbers lets each of them write about all of you. Professors write a lot of these letters, so this is a kindness, not an imposition.
  5. What to emphasize. For your PI, the sessions you run and the protocols you troubleshoot. For the psychology professor, the review sessions you started. If a program wants something particular, such as independence or clinical research, say so. And tell all of them you have not decided between an MD and an MD-PhD: some programs are built for future PhDs, and a letter that settles the question for you can work against you there.

Managing it afterwards

  • Add each recommender under Who is writing your letters on My Applications, and update their status as they reply. Note anything program-specific in that program's notes.
  • Most portals email the recommender a link only after you submit your part, so submit early. Seattle Children's closes 4 January and takes letters until 19 January. Submit it before you leave State College in December, and if its portal works this way, your PI has the link before the holidays.
  • Send a reminder ten days before each deadline if the portal still shows the letter as outstanding. For anything due in January, send it before you leave State College for winter break instead: professors are hard to reach over the holidays.
  • Thank them afterwards, and tell them the outcome either way. You will probably ask the same people again for medical school.

The honest timing note

A letter requested on 2 January for a 15 January deadline will be written in a hurry and will read like it. The same professor, asked in November, writes a better letter about the same review sessions. The quality difference is entirely in the lead time.

guides.title: Emailing a lab
guides.html:
The highest-return thing on this site, and almost nobody does it.

Many summer programs ask applicants to name preferred mentors, and a fair number of placements come down to a faculty member saying "I would take this student." At NIH it is the whole process. The Summer Internship Program has no central selection: individual investigators choose their own interns, starting in early January, so an email to an NIH lab is part of applying.

Several places on this site are reachable mainly this way: UCSF pediatrics, which has no undergraduate application; the UC Davis MIND Institute, where a direct lab email works better than the central application; and the places near home that have not posted a 2027 summer application with a deadline (Children's National, Georgetown, George Washington and Inova). One is the opposite: the Boston Children's epilepsy internship asks that questions go only to its internship address and never to lab members, so apply through its page instead. That page still shows last cycle's dates, so check it from early January.

A good cold email takes fifteen minutes. Send three or four per program you seriously want, earliest deadline first, and three to five to NIH labs, ideally before Thanksgiving and at the latest before winter break. Start with the programs rated Strong fit or Good fit, and read the For you line on each before you write.

The rules

  1. Short. Under 200 words. They are reading it on a phone between meetings.
  2. Specific. Name one of their papers and say something true about it. Generic praise is worse than none.
  3. Ask for one thing. Not "please mentor me for the summer", just whether they are taking a summer student.
  4. Answer "who pays" and "when" before they ask. Those are the first two questions in a PI's head. Name the program you are applying through and say that it pays your stipend, then give the dates you are free. An email that answers both reads as a student who can be slotted into a plan. One that leaves them open reads as a request for money and a scheduling problem.
  5. Attach the CV. One PDF, named Lastname-Firstname-CV.pdf, built from the CV skeleton.
  6. Subject line that survives a crowded inbox.
  7. No follow-up for ten days. Then exactly one, and never a third. If day ten falls over the holidays, send it in the first week of January.

Template

Subject: Summer 2027 [PROGRAM] applicant interested in [THEIR TOPIC]

Dear Dr. [LAST NAME],

I am a Penn State junior majoring in Integrative Science with a psychology minor, and I am applying to [PROGRAM NAME] for summer 2027. I would like to work in your lab.

I read your [YEAR] paper on [THE FINDING, not the title]. [ONE SENTENCE THAT SHOWS YOU READ IT.]

Since August 2025 I have been a research assistant in Dr. [YOUR PI]'s depression and anxiety lab, running participant sessions, coding data, troubleshooting study protocols and working on technology-based emotion tracking. I hold CITI certificates in social and behavioral human subjects research and Good Clinical Practice. I am also a volunteer EMT and have responded to more than 100 emergency calls.

[PROGRAM NAME] pays a stipend, so I would not need lab funding. I am free full time from [START DATE] to [END DATE]. [IF YOU CAN COMMUTE:] I live in Northern Virginia, so I do not need housing.

Are you taking a summer student in 2027? If the application asks for a preferred mentor, I would like to name you, with your permission.

My CV is attached. Thank you for your time.

[FULL NAME]

Penn State, Class of 2028

[EMAIL] · [PHONE]

The paper sentence is the one only you can write: what surprised you, a question it raised, or how it connects to the mood and emotion work in your own lab.

The background paragraph fits the labs you will email most, the ones that study people. Keep the CITI sentence for all of them: that training is the gate on work with participants or patients, and most undergraduates have none. Then fit the last sentence to the lab:

  • Clinical or hospital research (Children's National, Inova, an NIH clinical study): keep the EMT sentence and add "In summer 2026 I was a medical assistant in family medicine, seeing up to 26 patients a day and handling vital signs, blood draws and vaccines." If you have added the biomedical CITI course by then, name it in the CITI sentence, since hospital studies mostly run on that track. Trim elsewhere to stay under 200 words.
  • A pediatric lab: swap in "I have also shadowed a pediatrician for more than five years."
  • A lab with no patient contact: swap in "As a teaching assistant for a 300-student introductory psychology course, I started review sessions on my own."
  • A bench lab: replace the CITI and EMT sentences with "I have not done bench research yet, but I have taken organic chemistry and biochemistry, and I have been a Biology Learning Assistant for 80 students."

The stipend sentence is the one most applicants leave out, and it changes how the whole email reads. Check the program page first: most programs on this site pay a stipend, but some post no amount and a few pay nothing, so write only what is true. Where you find no program to name, as so far at Georgetown, George Washington and Inova, cut that sentence and the preferred-mentor line. Make the subject "Summer 2027 research, undergraduate interested in [THEIR TOPIC]", say in your first line that you are looking for summer research, and ask whether the lab has a summer program you could apply through.

The housing sentence is for labs you can reach from home: NIH, Janelia (if Penn State is a partner school for HHMI's Cech Fellows Program, its route for summer undergraduates), Inova and anywhere in DC. Baltimore is about 70 minutes each way, so keep it there only if you mean to make that drive, and cut it everywhere else. The living-at-home rule is why the labs near home are worth extra emails.

For NIH, name the Summer Internship Program and leave out the stipend sentence: NIH sets the stipend, and its PIs know how it is paid. Say instead whether you have submitted the application, which closes January 26 at noon Eastern. Dates are set with your PI, anywhere between May 10 and August 31. Name the same PIs in your cover letter.

Finding the right PI

Before you search, ask the people you have worked with whether they can point you to anyone doing the work you want: your lab's PI, the pediatrician you have shadowed for more than five years, the doctors from your medical assistant summer. An introduction from any of them beats a cold email.

  1. Open the program page, find the faculty or mentor list.
  2. No list? Search the department site for your topics: child anxiety and depression, developmental psychology, developmental and behavioral pediatrics, pediatric neurology. For NIH, search the Intramural Research Program by topic and look at the institute: NICHD for child health, NIMH for mood and anxiety, NINDS for neurology.
  3. Open two or three recent papers from each candidate on PubMed. If the abstracts bore you, you have saved yourself a summer.
  4. Check they are actually active. A lab whose last paper was 2019 may be winding down.
  5. Get the email from the faculty page, not from a paper's corresponding-author line, which is often stale.

What a reply looks like

  • "Yes, name me": excellent. Put it in the application immediately and say so explicitly: "Dr. X has agreed to host me." That line is worth a lot. At NIH, a yes means the PI will look for your application, so make sure it is submitted.
  • "I am not taking students but talk to Dr. Y": a warm introduction. Use it.
  • "Apply through the central program": neutral, but you are now a name they have seen rather than one of 400 files.
  • Silence: the normal outcome. Not personal. Send more.

Worth knowing

Expect most emails to go unanswered. Ten emails producing one "yes" is a good rate, and that one yes can decide the summer. The failure mode is not sending them at all.

guides.title: Why this program
guides.html:
The only part of the application that cannot be reused, which is exactly why it carries so much weight. A committee can tell in one sentence whether you looked at their page for ninety seconds or for twenty minutes. It is paragraph 4 of your master personal statement, the one that changes every time.

Budget 20-30 minutes per program. That is the whole cost.

What goes in it

Three things, in roughly 100-150 words:

  1. Something only true of this program. A named faculty member, a center, a specific resource, the structure of the summer.
  2. Why that matches what you want to do. The connection stated explicitly: do not make the reader infer it. Keep your question at the center, how mood and anxiety disorders show up in children, and tilt it toward the brain for a neurology lab or toward patients for a clinical program. Summer 2027 is your last summer of college, so if a program would help you decide between an MD and an MD-PhD, say so.
  3. What you would bring. One line, concrete, picked for the program:
    • A lab that studies people: you run participant sessions, code data and troubleshoot study protocols, and you hold three CITI certificates most undergraduates do not have.
    • A clinical or hospital program: more than 100 emergency calls as a volunteer EMT, or a summer as a medical assistant seeing up to 26 patients a day.
    • A pediatric program: more than five years of shadowing a pediatrician.
    • A bench lab: none of this is bench work, so say so, name the chemistry and biochemistry courses behind you, and add [WHAT CARRIES OVER TO THE BENCH]. Never imply bench skills you do not have.

The research, in four steps

  1. Open the program on the site and read its For you line, a fair place to start. Then open the program's own page and find the faculty or mentor list. This is the part worth the time.
  2. Pick two or three names whose work genuinely interests you. Labs that study people, children especially, are where your experience counts most.
  3. Look up one recent paper from each on PubMed. Read the abstract properly and skim the figures.
  4. Write the paragraph naming one or two of them and what specifically draws you. The same reading feeds a cold email to that PI, wherever the program welcomes one.

A worked example

Vague, could be sent anywhere:

I am excited to apply to your program because of its strong reputation in pediatric research and the excellent mentorship it provides. I believe this program would help me grow as a researcher and prepare me for medical school.

Specific, could only be sent to the Yale Child Study Center:

I am applying to the Undergraduate Developmental Science Summer Internship because the Child Study Center runs it with the Department of Pediatrics, and I want to work where developmental psychology meets pediatrics. [FACULTY MEMBER]'s [YEAR] paper on [AGE GROUP OR CONDITION] found [SPECIFIC FINDING], which surprised me because [HONEST REACTION]. In the Depression and Anxiety Lab at Penn State I run participant sessions and code data for research on how mood disorders show up in movement and affect, and since [THE MOMENT IT STARTED] I have wanted to know [YOUR QUESTION ABOUT CHILDREN]. I would come in able to run participant sessions under a human-subjects protocol, with CITI training in human subjects research and Good Clinical Practice, and I am most interested in [THE METHOD OR AGE GROUP THAT LAB STUDIES].

The second version is not better writing. It is better research. Everything outside the brackets is already true of you. The brackets are the reading and your own question.

Per-program angles

Pulled from the program data, for programs whose work is close to yours. Use them as the starting point. Seattle Children's closes first, on January 4, so write that one first.

ProgramThe thing to nameWhere you connect
Seattle Children'sA lab or research area from their page. The page says first-time research interns are prioritized.This would be your first research internship, which counts for you here. Say so plainly, then spend the rest on the lab.
Penn UCSPThe clinical question you want to work on. It is nine weeks on a clinical research project with an expert clinical investigator, plus statistics workshops in epidemiology and biostatistics.It is built for students aiming at an MD, PhD or MD-PhD, so your undecided answer fits: say what the summer would help you decide. You already code data, and the statistics are the next step.
Yale Child Study CenterThe lab, and the age group or condition it studies. The application is a one-page letter of interest for up to 12 places, so this paragraph is its center.The worked example above. Tie the lab to the mood and anxiety work you already do.
NIH SIPThe institute and two or three intramural labs: NICHD for child health, NIMH for mood and anxiety, NINDS for neurology. Investigators choose their own interns, so your cover letter is the paragraph that matters. Name the PIs you have emailed.Your lab's mood and anxiety work points to NIMH, your pediatric interest to NICHD and pediatric neurology to NINDS. Lead with one.
Strong Children's, RochesterThe pediatric specialty. You are placed with a faculty mentor in the specialty you pick, and the ten weeks end in a poster session for the whole Department of Pediatrics. Short answers stand in for a personal statement, and review is rolling, so earlier is better.Pick the specialty nearest your question and tie it to your shadowing and your lab. The poster would be your first, and wanting to present is worth saying.
CHOP CRISSPThe track, and a faculty member in it. Thirty students a summer, split across basic, clinical and behavioral tracks. An information session (December 8 at 11 a.m. or January 12 at 3 p.m.) is worth attending before you write.Participant sessions, data coding and emotion tracking are behavioral research. Everyone also gets clinical shadowing, which you have done for more than five years, so spend the words on the research.
St. Jude POEPediatric cancer and catastrophic disease, and the laboratory or computational work you want. Clinical research matches are reserved for medical students, so asking for clinical work asks for the one thing they cannot offer you.Your lab job should meet their rule that you already have research experience outside the classroom. It is human-subjects work, not bench work, so say so in one sentence, with what carries over. Check the four start dates (May 10, 17 or 24, or June 1) before you spend the twenty minutes.
Kennedy KriegerThe condition or age group, and the lab or center. Its research covers pediatric developmental disabilities, neurodevelopment and rehabilitation.This is developmental and behavioral pediatrics, which you want to study, so say which part and why. Your human-subjects work is what you bring.
UC Davis MIND InstituteOne condition and one lab. It studies neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism, fragile X and ADHD, and a direct lab email works better there than the central application, so this paragraph becomes the middle of that email.Your lab studies how mood disorders show up in movement and affect. Say what you want to learn about how [THE CONDITION] shows up in a child's behavior.
Boston Children's epilepsy labDr. Loddenkemper's pediatric epilepsy and EEG work. It is a single lab, so name one recent paper. Questions go only to the internship address on its page, never to lab members.Pediatric neurology is the interest to lead with. Say which of the lab's methods would be new to you, and offer what you have: participant sessions, data coding, protocol troubleshooting.

Umbrella programs need a paragraph about the piece, not the umbrella. Each Amgen Scholars host runs its own application, so write about that campus. Johns Hopkins Pathway lets you apply to several divisions, NeuroSIP among them, so give each its own reason. The Leadership Alliance ranks three of its 20 sites in one application, so name all three and say why each. Amgen and the Leadership Alliance are built for students heading to a PhD or MD-PhD, so write them only if the MD-PhD is a real question for you.

Check before sending

  • Program name spelled correctly, and it is the right program
  • At least one faculty member, lab or center named
  • At least one specific paper, finding, or resource referenced
  • No sentence that would survive a find-and-replace of the institution name
  • The "what I bring" line is concrete, not a feeling
  • Nothing suggests bench skills, a poster or a publication you do not have

guides.title: How to use all this
guides.html:
Everything in here is a starting point, not a finished document, but it starts from you: the templates are built around your own lab, certificates and clinical work. The parts in [SQUARE BRACKETS] are the parts only you can fill in, such as a story, a name or a number, and they are the parts a reader actually cares about.

What the site knows about you. It is built for you alone, from your lab work, CITI training, clinical hours, shadowing and teaching, what you want to study, and the fact that home is in Loudoun County. Every program carries a fit rating for you (Strong fit, Good fit, Possible or Weak fit), and its For you note says why. Fit is not the same as odds, which each program shows separately. Programs within reach of home are marked too, since living at home means no rent.

The one idea worth internalizing

Almost every applicant writes some version of "I have always loved working with children and I am eager to learn." Selection committees read hundreds of those. They are not evidence of anything.

What gets someone selected is specificity: a particular question you find interesting, a particular reason this lab can answer it, and some evidence you can be useful in a lab for ten weeks. You have the raw material for two of those already. Your question comes from where your lab and your years of shadowing meet: how mood and anxiety disorders show up in children. Your evidence is more than a year of running participant sessions, coding data and troubleshooting study protocols, with CITI training most undergraduates do not have. The reason a particular lab can answer your question is the part you research, one program at a time. One concrete sentence about a paper you read beats three paragraphs of enthusiasm.

What to build, in order

Letters are the most urgent, because they are the only thing here that runs on somebody else's calendar, and the first ones are due in January. Each request goes out with your CV, so the CV comes first, and the skeleton already has your lab, your certificates and your clinical work in place.

#ThingTimeReuse
1CV2 hours onceEvery letter request, lab email and application
2Recommendation requests30 min per recommenderSame letter goes everywhere
3Official transcript15 min to order, days to arriveEvery program that insists on an official copy
4Master personal statement4-6 hours once~80% reusable
5Cold emails to PIs15 min eachHighest return, lowest effort
6Per-program paragraph20-30 min eachNever reusable. This is the point

Guides worth reading before writing:

  • The timeline: what to do between now and February
  • How to actually get picked: what these committees weigh, and your own strengths and gaps
  • Reading a program page: finding the real requirements fast, and the living-at-home rule

The site around these documents

These guides sit inside a site, and a few parts of it are easy to miss:

  • The Plan is the page for a normal day: what is open, what is due next, your strongest fits, what the weekly check found on Monday, and which sites it cannot read.
  • All Programs has every program with its fit rating, and filters for research area, pay, housing and Can live at home. Sort it by fit to see your best matches first. Open a program for its For you note, eligibility, stipend, housing and requirements checklist.
  • My eligibility starts with your year and citizenship filled in, and nothing on the site rules you out on either. It is also where the site explains how it judges fit.
  • My Applications tracks each application, and its Who is writing your letters panel keeps track of your recommenders.
  • Back it up. Your progress is saved in this browser only. Press Backup at the top of the page once a week and keep the file somewhere safe. Restore brings it back on a new laptop or after you clear your browser.
  • Add to calendar downloads every opening date and deadline as a calendar file. Export spreadsheet downloads the whole list.
  • Your Claude kit has the files to attach to a Claude chat so it can help you fill in forms and draft emails.

The highest-return thing on this whole list

Cold-emailing PIs. Many programs let you name a preferred mentor, and plenty of placements are effectively decided by whether a specific faculty member said "I would take this student." At NIH it is the whole process: investigators choose their own interns, starting in early January, and Bethesda is a commute from home. Three or four short, specific emails per program you seriously want, and three to five to NIH labs before winter break, move the odds more than another round of polishing the personal statement. Start with the programs rated Strong fit or Good fit. The template already has your background paragraph, so your fifteen minutes go on the one sentence only you can write, about their paper. Template here.
